# cannot enable php8.2 with Apache2 compiled from sources

When you compile Apache from source, particularly alongside a custom OpenSSL build, the standard Debian/Ubuntu packaging utilities like `a2enmod` often fail to function as expected. The core issue in your scenario isn't necessarily that PHP is missing, but rather that the integration mechanism relies on finding specific `.so` files and configuration snippets in paths that a source-built Apache does not search by default.

The command `sudo a2enmod php8.2` attempts to modify `/etc/apache2/mods-available/php8.2.load` and symlink it to the mods-enabled directory. This process assumes that Apache is looking for PHP modules at `/usr/lib/php/...` or similar standard library paths, and that the configuration file includes a line pointing to `LoadModule`. However, if you compiled Apache from source in `/usr/local/apache2`, your binary is likely hardcoded to look for modules relative to its own installation prefix (e.g., `/usr/local/apache2/modules/`).

If you run `sudo a2enmod php8.2` and see no changes or errors, it usually means the module loader isn't finding the PHP Shared Object (`.so`) file in the expected location. When you request `/test.php` and only see raw code, Apache has successfully served the static file because the PHP handler is not registered in the `httpd.conf` or its included configuration files.

To resolve this, you must manually ensure that the PHP module is loaded by your custom-built Apache. First, verify where the PHP module was installed during the compilation process. If you followed a standard tutorial for compiling PHP 8.2 with OpenSSL, the `.so` file is likely located at `/usr/local/lib/php/20240924/php8.so` or similar, depending on your specific `./configure` flags and build options.

You need to explicitly add a `LoadModule` directive in your Apache configuration. Open your main config file (often found in `/usr/local/apache2/conf/httpd.conf`) or the include directory used by your source build. Add the following line, ensuring the path matches exactly where your PHP module resides:

```apache
LoadModule php_module /usr/local/lib/php/20240924/php8.so
```

Next, you must define a handler for files with the `.php` extension. Without this, Apache treats `.php` files as plain text, which explains why you are seeing the raw code in your browser. Add these directives to your `httpd.conf`:

```apache
AddType application/x-httpd-php .php
<FilesMatch \.php$>
    SetHandler application/x-httpd-php
</FilesMatch>
```

You also need to ensure that PHP's internal configuration is included. If you installed PHP with the `--enable-mbstring` or similar options, the `php.ini` file should be loaded via an `Include` directive:

```apache
Include /usr/local/lib/php/20240924/php.ini
```

Regarding your observation about `a2enmod`: it is normal for this command to make no visible changes if it cannot locate the module definition files in `/etc/apache2/mods-available`. Source-built software often bypasses these system directories entirely, installing everything under `/usr/local`. In such cases, you must manage your configuration manually.

If you are planning to stream a video using FFPlay over HTTPS with your custom OpenSSL, ensure that your SSL certificates are correctly configured in the `ssl.conf` or an equivalent file within your source build's config directory. You will need to verify that the `LoadModule ssl_module` is present and that your `SSLCertificateFile` and `SSLCertificateKeyFile` point to valid paths relative to your custom installation.

A common pitfall when mixing source-built Apache with system-installed PHP (or vice versa) is a mismatch in the OpenSSL versions. Since you mentioned using a custom OpenSSL version, ensure that the `openssl.so` library linked during the PHP compilation matches the one provided by your custom build. If they differ, PHP may fail to initialize silently or throw fatal errors when accessed via `phpinfo()`.

For a robust setup involving streaming and secure connections, consider isolating your SSL configuration in a dedicated file included at the end of your main config to keep things organized. This approach minimizes conflicts between system packages and custom compilations.
